nameStory: Cuthona nana gets its scientific name from the genus Cuthona, which honors early nudibranch researchers, combined with 'nana' meaning 'dwarf' in Latin. This tiny sea slug truly lives up to its diminutive name, being one of the smaller members of its family.
description: Cuthona nana is a tiny sea slug that belongs to a group called nudibranchs - marine snails that have lost their shells and developed colorful, finger-like projections called cerata on their backs. These delicate creatures are soft-bodied and translucent, with cerata that help them breathe and digest food. Like other nudibranchs, they're carnivorous, feeding on small marine organisms like hydroids. They're quite small, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length.

idTips.label: Cerata arrangement
idTips.description: Look for clusters of finger-like projections (cerata) arranged in rows along the back - these feel soft and jelly-like if gently touched in tide pools

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, usually under 10mm long - about the size of a small fingernail or rice grain

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Translucent, soft body that appears almost glass-like when submerged, with a smooth, slippery feel

idTips.label: Head tentacles
idTips.description: Two pairs of tentacles on the head - oral tentacles near the mouth and longer rhinophores that sense chemicals in the water

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces using a muscular foot, leaving a barely visible slime trail

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and on rocky substrates where hydroids grow. Look for them crawling on seaweeds, under overhangs, or in crevices during low tide. They prefer areas with good water circulation and abundant small prey.

seasonality.spring: May become more active as water temperatures rise and food sources become abundant. Best time to spot them during spring low tides.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when warm waters support peak feeding and reproduction. Look for them in tide pools during calm, clear days.
seasonality.fall: Still observable but may become less active as temperatures cool. Late fall storms can wash specimens into unusual locations.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed due to harsh conditions and reduced activity. May retreat to deeper, more protected waters.

funFact: Despite having no shell for protection, nudibranchs like Cuthona nana can steal stinging cells from the creatures they eat and store them in the tips of their cerata, essentially weaponizing their own backs with recycled armaments!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small nudibranchs, but the specific arrangement and number of cerata help distinguish species. A hand lens or magnifying glass is often needed for confident identification of these tiny creatures.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' - though what look like gills are actually multipurpose cerata that handle breathing, digestion, and defense all in one. Many people are surprised to learn these colorful creatures are actually snails without shells.
compareHints: Since no other Cuthona species are recorded in the New England dataset, compare with other small aeolid nudibranchs in the family Cuthonidae. Cuthona nana is distinguished by its particularly small size and specific cerata arrangement. Other family members may be larger or have differently shaped or colored cerata, making careful observation of these projections key to identification.
